source.title: HLAT: High-quality Large Language Model Pre-trained on AWS Trainium
source.authors: Haozheng Fan; Hao Zhou; Guangtai Huang; Parameswaran Raman; Xinwei Fu; Gaurav Gupta; Dhananjay Ram; Yida Wang; Jun Huan

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates downstream-task performance across training checkpoints and tokens, a different measurement from fitting scaling laws, and reports how task performance changes during training.
record.gate_note: The paper does not fit held-out-loss scaling laws or compare compute-optimal allocations. Training-loss curves are not held-out loss. Final comparisons with other models in Table II are not scaling-law tests and are not included as rows. Intermediate task curves are shown in figures without extractable numerical values.
record.test_reason: A model-training report, not a scaling-law study. Its intermediate-checkpoint evaluations (Sec. V-B, Figs. 3-4) give qualitative evidence on V6: whether downstream scores improve smoothly with training tokens and track training loss. The evidence is weak: two model sizes, figure-only curves and no fitted relationship. Hoffmann et al. is only cited in related work.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Additional points: the authors' main conclusion is that Trainium can pre-train LLMs of quality on par with LLaMA/OpenLLaMA at lower cost. The downstream-trajectory remarks are secondary. The authors also argue that broad evaluation suites are needed, since a single validation set may not reflect downstream performance.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains 7B and 70B models and evaluates intermediate checkpoints over training tokens; it does not fit held-out-loss scaling laws or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream trajectories vary by task; World Knowledge shot-count trends for HLAT-7B are reported as similar across zero-shot, 3-shot and 5-shot. HLAT-70B's final-stage results also follow a training-data upsampling change.

fits_no_version.finding: Training cross-entropy falls rapidly over the first ~250B tokens, then declines log-linearly, for both 7B and 70B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within a single run, training loss declines log-linearly in tokens after an initial fast phase.

record.problems: The paper reports only two model sizes and does not fit scaling exponents or test extrapolation. The loss curve is training loss, not held-out loss. Intermediate downstream curves are figures without extractable numerical values or uncertainty estimates; task trends differ, and the HLAT-70B late-stage evaluation follows a data-mixture change.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were omitted. Final benchmark comparisons in Table II and checkpoint-averaging comparisons in Table IV are not measurements of downstream predictability across scale or training loss.

untested.parts: Held-out loss power laws in N, D or C. Only training loss for two runs is shown, with no fit.
Extrapolation from small runs to large ones.
Effect of model shape at fixed parameter count.
A sweep across model scale, a fitted relation to pretraining loss, and prediction of larger runs. The study gives only within-run trajectories for 7B and 70B.
Fitted exponents and their dependence on setup or fitting choices.

missing.what: General statement that on most benchmarks performance improves steadily and correlates with training loss

record.verdict_notes: Weak evidence for V6. There are only two sizes, curves are figure-only and no predictive fit is made; the reported link to loss is qualitative. The upsampling rows were moved to none. Table II gives a 7B vs 70B comparison, but it is excluded under rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out loss power laws across parameter count, tokens or compute; several orders of magnitude.
Whether fits from smaller runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as compute varies.
Effects of depth, width and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities and training regimes, including repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer.
The study tracks downstream performance over training tokens for two model sizes; it does not test performance across a model-scale sweep or fit a predictive relationship to pretraining loss.
It reports no fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal split, and does not assess their dependence on fit choices.

relationships.condition: Commonsense Reasoning and World Knowledge over training tokens; most benchmarks per text
relationships.reason: WK rises almost linearly with tokens (r5) and CR rises with saturation (r4, r12). The text says most benchmarks improve steadily and correlate with training loss; this part is text-based, not a row.
relationships.display_finding: World knowledge increased almost linearly with tokens, commonsense reasoning improved with saturation, and most benchmarks reportedly improved steadily and correlated with training loss.

relationships.reason: Math stays near-flat for about 1T tokens, then improves sharply (r7), so early checkpoints would not predict it.
relationships.display_finding: GSM8K performance remained nearly flat for about 1T tokens before improving sharply, making early-checkpoint extrapolation unreliable.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: HLAT-7B World Knowledge evaluation across training tokens
reader_labels.reason: World Knowledge performance is described as increasing almost linearly with tokens, with similar trends across the tested shot counts (r5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Commonsense Reasoning and HLAT-7B math evaluation across training tokens
reader_labels.reason: Commonsense performance saturates later, while math improves very gradually at first and then rises significantly, showing task-dependent trajectories (r4, r7).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Math, coding and MMLU improve after a deliberate change to the data mixture; these results do not establish a general scale- or loss-based prediction rule (r18-r20).
